17151308.title: 2025_Enderlin_tornado
17151308.extract:
# 2025 Enderlin tornado

The **2025 Enderlin tornado** was a violent tornado that struck rural areas near Enderlin, North Dakota, on the night of June 20, 2025. The tornado was part of a larger severe weather outbreak and derecho event that affected the Upper Midwest and Northern Great Plains. It is notable for being the first tornado in the United States to be rated **EF5** on the Enhanced Fujita scale since the Moore, Oklahoma, tornado in 2013, ending a 12-year period without a confirmed EF5 tornado .

The tornado touched down late in the evening and tracked for approximately 12 miles (19 km), reaching a maximum width of over one mile . It resulted in three fatalities and caused extensive damage to rural homesteads, vegetation, and railroad infrastructure . While initially rated as an EF3, the National Weather Service (NWS) upgraded the tornado to EF5 status on October 6, 2025, following an extensive forensic analysis of wind speeds required to derail and loft heavy railway cars .

## Meteorological synopsis

On June 20, 2025, a volatile atmospheric setup developed over the Northern Plains, characterized by an unstable air mass and favorable wind shear profiles for supercell thunderstorms . The Storm Prediction Center had highlighted the risk for severe weather, including tornadoes and damaging winds, across the region .

During the late evening hours, supercell thunderstorms developed in southeastern North Dakota. These storms were part of a complex system that eventually evolved into a derecho—a widespread, long-lived wind storm—that produced wind gusts exceeding 100 mph (160 km/h) across North Dakota and Minnesota . The specific supercell responsible for the Enderlin tornado formed in a high-instability environment capable of supporting strong rotation .

The tornado touched down at approximately 11:02 p.m. CDT, about 3 miles south of Enderlin in Ransom County . It tracked northeastward, then turned north and eventually northwest before dissipating at 11:21 p.m. CDT near Alice in Cass County . The tornado was on the ground for 19 minutes and had a path length of 12.1 miles . At its peak intensity, the tornado reached a width of approximately 1.05 miles (1,850 yards) .

## Impact and casualties

The tornado caused catastrophic damage along its path through rural Ransom and Cass counties. Three people were killed by the storm: two men and one woman . The fatalities occurred at two separate locations near Enderlin . Authorities noted that the nocturnal nature of the tornado likely contributed to the danger, as many residents were asleep or had limited visibility of the approaching storm . No other major injuries were reported, although the broader storm system caused widespread power outages affecting over 30,000 customers in North Dakota and 54,000 in Minnesota .

### Structural and environmental damage
Approximately ten homes were damaged or destroyed by the tornado . One farmstead was described by damage surveyors as having its foundation "swept clean," with debris scattered downwind, an indicator of extreme wind intensity .

The tornado inflicted severe damage on vegetation. In the Maple River valley, a forest was largely obliterated; trees were snapped, uprooted, and debarked. Surveyors noted a "sandpapering" effect on the remaining tree stubs, a phenomenon often associated with violent tornadoes where high-velocity debris scours bark from wood .

### Railroad damage
A significant portion of the damage analysis focused on a Canadian Pacific Kansas City (CPKC) freight train that was struck by the tornado south of Enderlin. The tornado derailed 33 train cars . Among the derailed stock were 19 fully loaded grain hopper cars, which can weigh up to 286,000 pounds (130,000 kg) each . These cars were tipped over by the wind. Additionally, an empty tanker car, estimated to weigh between 50,000 and 90,000 pounds, was lofted and thrown approximately 476 feet (145 meters) from the tracks .

## Rating and analysis

Immediately following the event, the National Weather Service in Grand Forks assigned the tornado a preliminary rating of **EF3**, with estimated peak winds of 160 mph (260 km/h) . This initial rating was based on available damage indicators at the time, primarily damage to frame homes and trees.

### Upgrade to EF5
On October 6, 2025, nearly four months after the event, the NWS Grand Forks office issued a revised statement upgrading the tornado to an **EF5**, the highest rating on the Enhanced Fujita scale . This upgrade raised the estimated peak wind speeds to greater than 210 mph (340 km/h) .

The upgrade was the result of a collaborative forensic investigation involving the NWS, wind damage experts, and the Northern Tornadoes Project at Western University in Canada . The investigation utilized advanced engineering models to analyze the force required to cause the observed damage to the train cars.

Key findings leading to the upgrade included:
* **Train Derailment Analysis:** Engineers calculated that wind speeds exceeding 210 mph were necessary to tip the fully loaded grain hopper cars and to loft the empty tanker car the measured distance of 475.7 feet .
* **Tree Damage:** Re-analysis of the damage along the Maple River identified extreme "sandpapering" and debarking of trees, as well as the displacement of tree root balls, consistent with wind speeds in the EF5 range .
* **Radar Correlation:** The calculated wind speeds correlated with high-velocity signatures observed on WSR-88D radar data from the Grand Forks site during the storm .

### Historical significance
The upgrade of the Enderlin tornado to EF5 status was significant within the meteorological community. It ended a record-breaking 12-year "drought" of EF5 tornadoes in the United States; the previous confirmed EF5 had occurred in Moore, Oklahoma, on May 20, 2013 .

This event marked the first EF5 tornado recorded in North Dakota since the 1957 Fargo tornado . It was also the deadliest tornado in the state since the F4 tornado that struck Elgin in 1978 .

## Aftermath

Following the tornado and the associated derecho, North Dakota Governor Kelly Armstrong issued a statewide disaster declaration to facilitate emergency response and recovery efforts . The storm system caused an estimated $6 million in damage to electrical infrastructure alone .

Recovery efforts were extensive, with volunteers assisting in debris cleanup in the Enderlin area . In September 2025, a request for a presidential disaster declaration was approved, allowing for Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) funding to assist affected counties, including Barnes, Ransom, and Cass . However, the distribution of federal aid faced delays due to the United States federal government shutdown that was ongoing at the time of the rating upgrade in October 2025 .

2.content:
The National Weather Service in Grand Forks, ND, has ruled that a tornado near Enderlin, ND, caused EF-5 level damage upon further investigation. This marks the end of 12 years without a surveyed EF-5 tornado in the U.S. The last time EF-5 damage was reported from a tornado was in May of 2013 in Moore, OK.

The tornado is estimated to have wind speeds greater than 210 miles per hour. This tornado was on the ground for 12.1 miles with a width of just over a mile! Sadly, this storm caused three fatalities.

![Image 1](https://media.weathernationtv.com/app/uploads/2025/10/Screenshot%202025-10-06%20104454-1759769110628.png)

Here is more on what led the NWS to upgrade its survey findings:

> _"The National Weather Service in Grand Forks conducted additional surveys and worked extensively with wind damage experts to further investigate the 20 June 2025 Enderlin, ND tornado #1. The estimated maximum wind speed of the Enderlin, ND tornado #1 is greater than 210 mph and occurred during the time of the train derailment south of Enderlin, ND. The analysis involved forensic damage wind speed estimates for tipping several fully-loaded grain hopper cars and lofting of tanker cars, including one empty tanker car that was tossed about 475.7 ft (145 m)."_

![Image 2](https://media.weathernationtv.com/app/uploads/2025/10/Screenshot%202025-10-06%20102949-1759768203710.png)We spoke with the National Weather Service in Grand Forks, ND, to learn more about the decision to upgrade the tornado rating and the factors that influenced the decision.

SET-UP
------

On June 20, 2025, a derecho brought wind gusts of 70 -105 mph to the north central U.S., spanning over 400 miles and leaving hundreds of thousands of households without power. Multiple long-track, destructive tornadoes were within this storm system.

A derecho is a long-lived severe wind event, with specific criteria about the length and width of the damaging wind swath. The [**SPC has a detailed page**](https://www.spc.noaa.gov/misc/AbtDerechos/derechofacts.htm) dedicated to these destructive windstorms. Several typically occur each year, though they can vary in intensity and area. A notable [**derecho ripped through Des Moines in 2020**](https://www.weathernationtv.com/news/one-year-ago-the-midwest-derecho), producing hurricane-force winds and widespread damage.

OTHER REPORTS
-------------

Wind gusts in North Dakota and Minnesota (as well as northern South Dakota) were impressive, many over hurricane strength. A wake-low also developed behind the leading edge, producing severe strength winds (58+ mph) in some locations for over an hour!

![Image 3](https://media.weathernationtv.com/app/uploads/2025/06/Screenshot%202025-06-21%20053620-1750505847379.png)Bemidji, Minnesota, was hit particularly hard in the overnight hours as an intense bout of winds moved through the area, with a tornado potentially embedded in the circulation. The Bemidji Regional Airport reported a gust to 106 mph, with widespread damage reported in the area.

![Image 4](https://media.weathernationtv.com/app/uploads/2025/06/Screenshot%202025-06-21%20053627-1750505847378.png)The widely spanning severe winds have left hundreds of thousands of households in the dark the following morning, with some counties reporting well over 60-60% of customers without power. As a reminder, if you're going to run a generator to power anything, keep it at least 25 feet away from any opening in your home, like windows and doors.![Image 5](https://media.weathernationtv.com/app/uploads/2025/06/1-1750541351436.png)

This was one of many severe weather events that pushed [North Dakota to break their yearly tornado record](https://www.weathernationtv.com/news/north-dakota-breaks-yearly-tornado-record).

At least three people dead from a tornado in North Dakota
=========================================================

    ![Image 3: NPR](https://npr.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/2b417b6/2147483647/strip/true/crop/138x46+0+0/resize/880x293!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fmedia.npr.org%2Fimages%2Fstations%2Flogos%2Fnpr.gif)

By Clare Marie Schneider

Published June 21, 2025 at 5:51 PM EDT

*   [Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/dialog/share?app_id=966144370871591&display=popup&href=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.whro.org%2F2025-06-21%2Fat-least-three-people-dead-from-a-tornado-in-north-dakota)
*   [Twitter](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.whro.org%2F2025-06-21%2Fat-least-three-people-dead-from-a-tornado-in-north-dakota&text=At%20least%20three%20people%20dead%20from%20a%20tornado%20in%20North%20Dakota)
*   [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/shareArticle?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.whro.org%2F2025-06-21%2Fat-least-three-people-dead-from-a-tornado-in-north-dakota&mini=true&title=At%20least%20three%20people%20dead%20from%20a%20tornado%20in%20North%20Dakota&summary=At%20least%20three%20residents%20were%20killed%20in%20the%20Enderlin%20area%20by%20a%20tornado%20on%20Friday%20night%20after%20storms%20hit%20North%20Dakota%20and%20Minnesota.&source=WHRO)
*   [Email](mailto:?body=At%20least%20three%20people%20dead%20from%20a%20tornado%20in%20North%20Dakota%0A%0Ahttps%3A%2F%2Fwww.whro.org%2F2025-06-21%2Fat-least-three-people-dead-from-a-tornado-in-north-dakota%0A%0AAt%20least%20three%20residents%20were%20killed%20in%20the%20Enderlin%20area%20by%20a%20tornado%20on%20Friday%20night%20after%20storms%20hit%20North%20Dakota%20and%20Minnesota.)

    ![Image 4: Severe storms struck Bismarck, N.D., and other areas of the state early on Saturday, leaving at least three dead.](https://npr.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/bde2643/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1568x1176+0+0/resize/880x660!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnpr.brightspotcdn.com%2Fdims3%2Fdefault%2Fstrip%2Ffalse%2Fcrop%2F1568x1176%2098%200%2Fresize%2F1568x1176%21%2F%3Furl%3Dhttp%3A%2F%2Fnpr-brightspot.s3.amazonaws.com%2F7b%2F37%2Fc913a37a41c78a2d434cb92da035%2Fap25172651912473.jpg)

Tanner Ecker/The Bismarck Tribune

/

via Associated Press

Severe storms struck Bismarck, N.D., and other areas of the state early on Saturday, leaving at least three dead.

At least three North Dakota residents were killed Friday night by a tornado that swept through the state overnight.

Storm chasers found two people killed as a result of the storm in rural Enderlin on Friday night, some 60 miles southwest of Fargo, N.D. That same night, The Enderlin Sheldon Fire Department found a third person dead from the storm, according to [a Facebook post](https://www.facebook.com/CassCountySO/posts/pfbid0VBut9k4H5NiqYoRwoqc3mS5K2cynSgC12DyZoaw2Lm36TTWRCMbKG1EuN7jnxUWTl?locale=en_GB) from the Cass County Sheriff's Office.

"As you look around, there's a lot of damage. A lot of residences were affected by the storm," Cass County sheriff Jesse Jahner, said [at a press conference Saturday morning](https://www.facebook.com/ValleyNewsLive/videos/1753744158878896). He confirmed two men and one woman died on Friday night and that authorities checked on residents and the impacted area Saturday morning. Jahner said, "we did not come across any other major injuries."

Jahner noted that because the tornado hit at night, residents might not have had enough time to prepare, contributing to the deaths.

Enderlin Sheldon Fire Department chief Jon Anderson said the department identified around ten homes damaged in the storm's path and that some livestock were lost from the storm as well. "There were a number of farmers out searching for cows early this morning," he said.

Anderson and Jahner agreed that the storm was the worst they've responded to in their careers.

Another round of severe storms may impact the area Saturday night and Sunday. "Hail and wind are the primary threat, but a tornado cannot be ruled out," the National Weather Service Grand Forks posted on X [Saturday morning](https://x.com/NWSGrandForks/status/1936327633341386800).

Severe storms with winds of more than 100 mph left major damage across a wide swath of northern Minnesota overnight as well, [reported MPR News](https://www.mprnews.org/story/2025/06/21/severe-storms-cause-major-damage-across-northern-minnesota-bemidji). In Minnesota, Bemidji was among the communities hit hard by the storms, with officials advising against unnecessary travel in the city and surrounding area on Saturday morning due to downed trees and power lines.

As of late Saturday afternoon, [over 19,000 people](https://poweroutage.us/area/state/north%20dakota) in North Dakota and [about 28,000 people](https://poweroutage.us/area/state/minnesota) in Minnesota were still without power according to PowerOutage.us.

EF5 tornadoon the Enhanced Fujita scaleMax width1,850 yards (1.05 mi; 1.69 km)Path length12.10 miles (19.47 km)Highest windsOfficial intensity: >210 mph (340 km/h)Unofficial intensity: >266 mph (428 km/h)(estimate from National Weather Service)[a]Overall effectsFatalities3[3]Injuries0[4]Areas affectedAreas near Enderlin, North Dakota, USPart of the tornado outbreak and derecho of June 19–22, 2025 and tornado outbreaks of 2025

On the night of June 20, 2025, a large and extremely violent EF5 tornado moved through rural North Dakota, United States, passing near the community of Enderlin. Part of a larger outbreak and derecho sequence that occurred across the northern Great Plains between June 19 and 22, the tornado, referred to as Enderlin Tornado #1 by the National Weather Service (NWS),[2][4][b] was the first to be rated EF5 on the Enhanced Fujita scale since the tornado that struck Moore, Oklahoma, on May 20, 2013, ending a 12-year-long period without tornadoes rated EF5. Throughout its short lifespan of only 16 minutes, it achieved a peak width of just over a mile (1.6 km) wide, and tracked a total length of 12.1 miles (19.5 km), with wind speeds in excess of 210 mph (340 km/h). It killed three people, becoming the deadliest tornado to occur in North Dakota since the F4 tornado that struck Elgin in 1978.
The tornado was given a preliminary rating of EF3, with the highest wind speeds estimated at 160 mph (260 km/h).[5] However, this rating was upgraded to EF5 following additional surveys and forensic damage analysis for the tipping and lofting of several fully-loaded grain hopper cars and empty tanker cars conducted in association with wind damage experts and researchers at the Northern Tornadoes Project, with peak winds needed to cause such damage estimated upwards of at least 266 mph (428 km/h).[6] The tornado also destroyed multiple farmhouses and obliterated a forest along the Maple River. A statewide disaster was declared by the Governor of North Dakota following the tornado outbreak. In September, federal disaster relief was approved, but was stalled amid the 2025 United States federal government shutdown. Locals and other organizations volunteered to help with the recovery efforts.

Meteorological synopsis[edit]
.mw-parser-output .hatnote{font-style:italic}.mw-parser-output div.hatnote{padding-left:1.6em;margin-bottom:0.5em}.mw-parser-output .hatnote i{font-style:normal}.mw-parser-output .hatnote+link+.hatnote{margin-top:-0.5em}@media print{body.ns-0 .mw-parser-output .hatnote{display:none!important}}Main article: Tornado outbreak and derecho of June 19–22, 2025 § Meteorological synopsis
On June 15, the Storm Prediction Center (SPC) on its Day 6 outlook forecasted that a shortwave, mid-level ridge would move into the upper Mississippi River Valley and remain over the region throughout June 20. Beneath the ridge, a moist and unstable airmass was expected to be in place from the lower to mid-Missouri River Valley, northeastward into the western Great Lakes region. Instability and deep-layer wind shear were sufficient for a localized severe weather threat, though uncertainties remained on where the greatest potential for convection was.[7]
A seasonally strong mid-level trough was forecast to eject over the Northern Plains on June 20, which featured moderate upper-level divergence to promote lift and deep-layer shear.[7] The Storm Prediction Center (SPC) Day 2 outlook mentioned that "a small area of uncapped and very unstable air mass, perhaps over northeast SD and southeast ND. Here, a conditional supercell and tornado risk will exist ... very large hail and tornadoes appear likely."[8]
At 8:15 p.m. on June 20, the SPC noted that storms developing over eastern North Dakota, while potentially elevated, were entering a favorable environment to become surface-based and pose a greater risk for hazards of severe weather. These storms followed to the southwest of a lone supercell already producing large hail. As these storms moved towards the Red River, favorable low-level wind conditions were forecast to support an increased threat of tornadoes, albeit in a smaller and localized region. At this time, forecasters noted that tornadoes could be strong, with the most likely peak wind speeds from any tornado being 120–150 mph (190–240 km/h).[9] A few tornadoes touched down before the Enderlin tornado, including an EF3 tornado near Spiritwood and two EF2 tornadoes near Valley City and Fort Ransom, respectively; both moved in a southeasterly direction towards the Enderlin area.[10][11] The SPC released a mesoscale discussion concerning this with the potential for EF2/EF3–strength tornadoes to occur as a result.[10]

Tornado summary[edit]
Formation and peak intensity[edit]
A radar scan of the tornado and parent supercell near peak intensity. Note the hook echo (left) and extremely powerful tornado vortex signature (right).
The tornado initially touched down at 11:02 p.m. Central Daylight Time (UTC–5) along 58th Street SE, 3.8 miles (6.1 km) south of Enderlin in Ransom County. After snapping tree branches at EF0 intensity at its touchdown point, the tornado intensified and widened as it moved east-northeastward across County Road 55 through open fields.[5][12] The tornado then impacted the ADM Edible Bean Specialties grain elevator facility at the corner of 136th Avenue SE and County Road 136 at EF2 strength, snapping large trees and destroying an outbuilding.[12] The tornado then began a rapid intensification and widening phase as it turned northeastward. It reached EF5 intensity as it crossed CPKC's Elbow Lake Subdivision southeast of Enderlin, derailing numerous train cars on a stopped freight train. Five train cars were lofted, and 28 more were tipped over.[4][12][13][14] A home that was on the edge of the path sustained minor EF0 damage to its roof as well.[12]
The tornado then turned north-northeastward, growing to its peak width of 1.05 miles (1.69 km). It blew over a cell tower that was anchored by four cables into the ground, completely scoured crop fields, and snapped large trees, debarking some of them. It also leveled an unoccupied farmhouse, shifted another house off its foundation, and damaged or destroyed outbuildings. Damage in this area was rated EF2 to EF3.[12] The tornado then inflicted violent EF4 damage to trees as it moved along the Maple River and approached ND 46. An entire forest of trees along the river was leveled, with only stubs of the trees left behind. Severe debarking of trees was also noted, with some of them being "sandpapered," and some trees were lofted with the root ball attached, including one whose original location could not be determined.[12]

Home east of Enderlin swept away at mid-range EF4 intensity, two fatalities were recorded here.
The violent tornado then crossed ND 46 into Cass County, and devastated two homes, with two deaths occurring in this area. The first home, along with a well-built detached garage nearby, was obliterated and swept away with all the debris scattered downwind of both structures. It was acknowledged that the tornado may have been even stronger at this location, but insufficient anchoring prevented a rating higher than mid-range EF4.[12] The second house, located approximately 300 yd (270 m) to the west of the first along 140th Avenue SE, along with nearby outbuildings, was leveled.[12][15] The tornado then crossed over the Maple River, leveling another swath of trees.[12]

Dissipation[edit]
The tornado then turned due north and paralleled 140th Avenue SE, snapping trees and damaging crops at EF2 strength. It also caused EF1 damage as it crossed along 52nd Street SE, shattering the windows of a home and inflicting roof damage to a mobile home.[12] The tornado then turned north-northwestward, leveling another farmhouse at high-end EF3 strength, and snapping numerous trees; one person was killed in the house.[5][12][15] After snapping more trees at EF2 strength, the tornado turned northwestward and toppled four tall steel electrical transmission towers at low-end EF3 strength; it also snapped wooden power poles in this area as it crossed County Road 38.[12][5] The tornado then quickly narrowed and weakened as it sharply looped back to the south along the southern end of the Utke Waterfowl Production Area, crossing County Road 16 twice, and snapping some additional hardwood tree trunks at EF2 strength before dissipating just west of the 50th Street SE and 138th Avenue SE intersection at 11:21 p.m. Central Daylight Time (UTC–5), approximately 5 miles (8.0 km) southwest of Alice.[12][5][16]

The tornado, seen southeast of Enderlin
Overall, the tornado was on the ground for 19 minutes, had a path length of 12.10 miles (19.47 km), and reached a peak width of 1.05 miles (1.69 km).[17] According to the Enderlin–Sheldon Fire Department, 10 homes sustained some form of damage from the storm.[18][19] Shortly after the dissipation of the Enderlin tornado, a second large tornado formed just east of the first tornado's path at 11:22 p.m. CDT. Moving southeast, this second tornado caused EF2 damage to trees and outbuildings across a 6.82 miles (10.98 km) path before dissipating at 11:34 p.m. CDT.[12]

Aftermath[edit]
Casualties and recovery efforts[edit]
EF4-rated root ball displacement caused by the tornado.
Governor of North Dakota Kelly Armstrong declared a statewide disaster following the tornado, activating the state's "Emergency Operations Plan".[18] On June 24, over 150 volunteers joined in a joint cleanup operation.[20][21] The International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement sent disaster teams to Enderlin to aid in recovery efforts,[22] and volunteers from the Northern Plains UAS Test Site deployed an Unmanned Aerial System to help residents find personal items that had been lost as a result of the tornado.[23][24] North Bank set up a fund for victims of the tornado, and the Enderlin Fire Department assisted in initial clean-up efforts.[25][26]
The town of Enderlin itself was not struck by the tornado, although it lost power due to the storm.[27] Debris fallout from the tornado extended to Moorhead, Minnesota, 40 miles (64 km) from where they originated. Here, a photograph and a tax return form, both belonging to two different people killed in the tornado, were found after the storm carried them there.[28]
The 2025 United States federal government shutdown, which was ongoing at the time of the tornado's upgrade to an EF5 rating, made disaster assistance unavailable until the shutdown ended;[29][30] President Donald Trump had approved Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) disaster relief to assist the month prior.[31]
The tornado killed three people, all in the vicinity of Enderlin.[32][16] The three deaths occurred at two different locations along the tornado's path.[33] It was the deadliest tornado to strike the state since 1978, when an F4 tornado killed five people in Elgin.[34][35][3]

Rating upgrade[edit]
The National Weather Service office in Grand Forks, North Dakota, originally gave the tornado an EF3 rating.[36] Peak winds were estimated to be around 160 miles per hour (260 km/h).[37]EF5-rated damage to several full grain train cars and empty tank cars tossed and derailed near Enderlin.
On October 6, 2025, the NWS Grand Forks, with assistance from several engineers including Timothy P. Marshall,[38] released a revised survey of the Enderlin tornado. Its final rating was upgraded to EF5 on the Enhanced Fujita scale, with maximum winds estimated to be over 210 miles per hour (340 km/h; 94 m/s).[4][13] The tornado also caused high-end damage in other areas, although the construction at these areas limited said damage points to being upgraded from high-end EF3 to mid-range EF4. The strong winds correlated to the indicated winds on the WSR-88D Storm-Relative Velocity data from the Grand Forks radar site.[4]
The intensity of the tornado was calculated from the distances the train cars were lofted and thrown. This new method was outlined in a study authored by a team of scientists and engineers of the Northern Tornadoes Project, and published in the peer-reviewed journal Monthly Weather Review in 2024.[39] In this study, researchers with the Northern Tornadoes Project found an empirical relationship between the distance large and compact objects, such as farm equipment and vehicles, were thrown by the tornado, and damage indicators corresponding to ratings on the Enhanced Fujita scale. The study used tornadoes throughout Canada as examples, and found that these tornadoes, which occurred near Alonsa, Manitoba on August 3, 2018, Scarth, Manitoba, on August 7, 2020, and Didsbury, Alberta, on July 1, 2023, were all most likely of EF5 intensity, based on Monte Carlo simulations on cumulative distribution functions showing the likelihood of lofting at each wind speed based on the weight and distance of objects lofted.[40]
In all, it was determined that 33 cars on the train derailed;[14] 19 of them were fully loaded grain hopper cars weighing up to 286,000 lb (130,000 kg) that were all tipped over, with one of them being pulled off the tracks and thrown into an adjacent field. The other 14 cars were empty tanker cars weighing up to 72,000 lb (33,000 kg). Four of the cars were thrown out into the field, including one that was tossed 600–1,000 ft (180–300 m), landing 475.7 ft (145.0 m) away from the previous tank car it was attached to. Wheel sets from the derailed cars detached at the locations where the cars came off the rails. Collaborating with wind damage experts and the Northern Tornadoes Project, the NWS determined that winds of 230 mph (370 km/h) were needed to tip over a fully loaded grain car and winds of over 266 mph (428 km/h) to throw a tank car 475.7 ft (145.0 m).[41]  In addition, extreme radar measurements were observed around the time that EF5-rated damage was being inflicted. It was also determined that the train cars were lofted twice as far as the EF5 threshold distance and four times heavier than the heaviest object model in the reanalysis. Prior to the reanalysis, the damage to the train cars had been left unrated since train cars are not standard damage indicators.[42][12]

Melinda Beerends, meteorologist in charge of the National Weather Service office in Grand Forks, stated that "In the last kind of 12 years, there's been several strong tornadoes that have come close, but there haven't been known damage indicators at that time to support the EF5 rating ... it's hard sometimes to get tornadoes to hit something."[43] The upgraded rating ended the EF5 drought that had begun following the May 2013 Moore, Oklahoma, tornado.[44] The tornado was additionally the first F5 or EF5-rated tornado to occur in the month of June in the United States since the 1992 tornado near Chandler, Minnesota.[45][46]

NORTH DAKOTA, USA — There has been a big shakeup in the meteorology world recently that has scientists and weather-enthusiasts in shock.

On June 20, a large and violent tornado touched down in Enderlin, North Dakota. It destroyed part of a forest along the Maple River, upended train cars, and severely damaged homes, causing three fatalities.

Initially, this tornado was rated an EF3. But due to work from the Northern Tornadoes Project of Western University in Ontario, the Canadian Severe Storms Laboratory, and wind damage experts, the National Weather Service upgraded the ranking to an EF5.

This is a big deal in the scientific community, as EF5 tornadoes are extremely rare. The last one occurred 12 years ago in 2013, when a massive and destructive tornado struck Moore, Oklahoma, and 24 people died.

Tornadoes are ranked using the Enhanced Fujita Scale. The EF scale rates tornadoes from 0 to 5. The rating is based on the damage the tornado causes, and the wind speeds are extrapolated from there, not a direct measurement of wind speeds or size. Therefore, a strong tornado that only impacts a corn field may yield a smaller rating than one that strikes a town due to a lack of damage evidence.

![Image 24](https://media.newscentermaine.com/assets/NCM/images/b393f217-5dbc-4e05-887f-d2777fe3028a/20251016T160122/b393f217-5dbc-4e05-887f-d2777fe3028a_16x9.jpg) ![Image 25](https://media.newscentermaine.com/assets/NCM/images/b393f217-5dbc-4e05-887f-d2777fe3028a/20251016T160122/b393f217-5dbc-4e05-887f-d2777fe3028a_1140x641.jpg)

Credit: NCM

Tornadoes do happen in Maine, but they're often few and far between. Maine averages only two tornadoes per year and has never seen a tornado above an EF2 ranking. The most recent tornadoes were a landspout in 2023 and an EF0 in 2020, which caused some damage in the towns of Hiram and Sebago.

The U.S.'s strongest tornado in 12 years hit North Dakota in June, National Weather Service says
================================================================================================

By Nick Lentz,

Nikki Nolan

[Nikki Nolan Meteorologist, CBS News and Stations](https://www.cbsnews.com/team/nikki-nolan/)

Nikki Nolan is a meteorologist for CBS News and Stations. She graduated from Metropolitan State University of Denver with a Bachelor of Science degree in Meteorology and has worked in national weather TV coverage since 2019.

[Read Full Bio](https://www.cbsnews.com/team/nikki-nolan/)

[Nikki Nolan](https://www.cbsnews.com/team/nikki-nolan/)

Updated on: October 6, 2025 / 5:32 PM CDT / CBS Minnesota

[Add CBS News on Google](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=cbsnews.com)

A deadly tornado that [ripped through a rural city in North Dakota in June](https://www.cbsnews.com/minnesota/news/bemidji-storm-damage-north-dakota-tornado-kills-3/) has been upgraded to an EF-5, the National Weather Service said Monday, marking the first U.S. twister with an EF-5 rating in 12 years.

The federal agency's Grand Forks, North Dakota, facility estimates the twister that touched down in the southeast city of Enderlin on June 20 had a maximum wind speed of over 210 mph. Wind speeds in a tornado need to reach at least 200 mph for it to be classified as an EF-5, the highest rating on the [Enhanced Fujita Scale](https://www.weather.gov/oun/efscale).

The initial estimate in the days after it happened was an EF-3.

Authorities said two men and a woman died during the tornado, which caused extensive tree damage, tipped several train cars fully loaded with grain and lifted tanker cars. The NWS said one tanker car was thrown just over 475 feet.

The severe weather event also destroyed a farm in the area, with the foundation of at least one of its buildings "considered to be swept clean," according to the NWS.

![Image 2: enderlin-nd-ef-5-tor-june-20-21-2025-1.png ](https://assets2.cbsnewsstatic.com/hub/i/r/2025/10/06/190a56af-ddf5-45cf-841e-8f38e4a0f771/thumbnail/620x349/04f487655e2ae9cfa57175edc1b5a8e7/enderlin-nd-ef-5-tor-june-20-21-2025-1.png#)

Tornado report in North Dakota from June 20, 2025, to June 21, 2025. WCCO

According to officials, the tornado lasted just under 20 minutes, from 11:02 p.m. to 11:21 p.m., and created a 12-mile path of destruction from Enderlin to Alice, North Dakota.

Enderlin is around 57 miles southwest of Fargo, North Dakota.

The last confirmed EF-5 tornado in the U.S. [touched down in Moore, Oklahoma](https://www.cbsnews.com/pictures/massive-tornado-hits-oklahoma/), on May 20, 2013, according to the [National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration](https://www.spc.noaa.gov/faq/tornado/f5torns.html).

![Image 3: Tornado Outbreak Slams Through Oklahoma ](https://assets2.cbsnewsstatic.com/hub/i/r/2025/10/06/b1cd65ce-5f65-450b-8f56-ccaa72fcde1f/thumbnail/620x406/cd5e205425557bbc7584dabae91f041d/gettyimages-169144295.jpg#)

\-MOORE, OK- MAY 20: Flipped vehicles are piled up outside the heavily damaged Moore Medical Center after a powerful tornado ripped through the area on May 20, 2013 in Moore, Oklahoma. The tornado, reported to be at least EF-4 strength and two miles wide, touched down in the Oklahoma City area on Monday killing at least 51 people. Brett Deering / Getty Images

The 2013 tornado [had wind speeds of up to 200 mph](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/massive-okla-tornado-had-windspeed-up-to-200-mph/). According to the NWS, it traveled over 14 miles, killed 24 people, injured over 200 others and damaged many structures.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

Three people killed in North Dakota after tornado hits upper midwest
====================================================================

This article is more than 5 months old

Officials say two men and a woman killed around town of Enderlin as region experiences powerful winds and hail

Associated Press

Sat 21 Jun 2025 23.20 BSTLast modified on Sun 22 Jun 2025 15.55 BST

[Share](mailto:?subject=ThreepeoplekilledinNorthDakotaaftertornadohitsuppermidwest&body=https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2025/jun/21/tornado-upper-midwest-north-dakota?CMP=share_btn_url)

Powerful winds – including a tornado – that swept across parts of the upper midwest left three people dead and a regional airport heavily damaged, while nearly 150 million Americans were under a heat advisory or warning as the weekend warmed up in much of the US.

A complex storm system wreaked havoc in parts of [North Dakota](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/north-dakota), northern Minnesota and northern Wisconsin, with reported tornadic activity, large hail and strong wind gusts, according to Brian Hurley, meteorologist with the National Weather Service’s Weather Prediction Center.

The Cass county sheriff, Jesse Jahner, said at a news conference on Saturday that two men and a woman were killed late on Friday at two locations around the town of Enderlin, North Dakota, about 40 miles (60km) south-west of Fargo. Thousands of households lost power.

Hours earlier the National Weather Service in Grand Forks [confirmed](https://x.com/NWSGrandForks/status/1936314523897467071) on social media that two deaths were attributed to a tornado that hit a home.

Timothy Lynch, lead forecaster with the NWS office in Grand Forks, said the storm was confirmed as a tornado but crews were still working to determine its strength and highest wind speeds. He said the storm hit the neighboring counties of Cass and Ransom.

“We still have people out investigating and gathering information on what happened. It was a pretty major event,” Lynch told the Associated Press.

Governor Kelly Armstrong said in a statement that the NWS confirmed a second tornado touched down near Spiritwood, which is about 80 miles west of Fargo. Armstrong issued a statewide disaster declaration to respond to the damage.

Heavy winds also swept across localized areas of [Minnesota](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/minnesota), and the NWS reported wind gusts of up to 106mph (171km/h) at Bemidji regional airport overnight.

“I cannot ever recall hearing a rushing wind like that!” Bemidji’s mayor, Jorge Prince, posted on Facebook in the early hours of Saturday. “Emerged from our basement to find our neighborhood with lots of trees down and several homes with severe damage.”

Prince also said officials were responding to many knocked-down power lines and several gas line leaks. Localized torrential rain flooded the city’s downtown and stalled vehicles, Beltrami’s county emergency management director, Christopher Muller, said.

Many Bemidji-area businesses posted on social media to say they were without power and closed for the day. Muller warned people to prepare for “long-term power outages” because of damage to infrastructure.

Hurley said that same storm moved on in a weakened state to parts of Michigan. It was expected to cross over lower Ontario and back into the United States to hit upstate New York on Saturday night into Sunday.

“Still wind and hail threat,” Hurley said of the enhanced risk to upstate New York. “It doesn’t look like it’s going to be as robust perhaps as we saw last night.”

Warm and dry conditions coupled with frequent thunderstorms and lightning have resulted in more than 100 fires in the state since Wednesday.

“A lot of those fires are in vast wilderness areas of Alaska where fire is allowed to take its natural course,” said Sam Harrel, an information officer with the state’s division of forestry and fire protection.

But some fires were threatening populated areas, prompting evacuations in the interior region. Among them was a go order issued on Friday for areas near Fairbanks, according to Harrel.

A fire burning about 30 miles north of the entrance to Denali national park and preserve also prompted an evacuation “due to escalating fire conditions”, the Denali borough said via Facebook.

“Numerous structures are now imminently threatened so aircraft including Air Tankers and helicopters are supporting the fire with retardant and water drops,” the borough added.

Harrel said the fire was not affecting the status of the park but the smoke could worsen air quality for visitors.

Enderlin ND Tornado Upgraded to EF-5: First in U.S. Since 2013 and Questions About Rating Consistency | Ryan Hall, Y'all
===============

3.title: RUYtNSB0b3JuYWRvIGRyb3VnaHQgZW5kcyBhcyBOV1MgdXBncmFkZXMgRW5kZXJsaW4gdG9ybmFkbw==
3.content:
![Image 1: EF-5 tornado: Black-and-white view of a street with houses and a lowered funnel cloud in the background.](https://earthsky.org/upl/2025/10/Enderlin-tornado-Jun-20-2025-ND-Ring-doorbell-Wikimedia-commons-e1759771659254.png)

A ring doorbell caught the Enderlin tornado in North Dakota on June 20, 2025. Almost 4 months later, the National Weather Service ([NWS](http://chrome-extension//efaidnbmnnnibpcajpcglclefindmkaj/https://www.weather.gov/media/fgf/Enderlin.pdf)) has upgraded it to an [EF-5 tornado](https://earthsky.org/earth/enhanced-fujita-scale-rates-tornado-strength/). This ends a 12-year drought where the U.S. didn’t see any tornadoes falling into the strongest classification. Image via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:June_20,_2025,_tornado_near_Enderlin,_North_Dakota.png) (public domain).

### EF-5 tornado drought over with Enderlin upgrading

For more than a decade, the United States had gone without an [EF-5 tornado](https://earthsky.org/earth/enhanced-fujita-scale-rates-tornado-strength/), the strongest category on the Enhanced Fujita (EF) Scale. This scale classifies tornado strength based on the damage they cause and estimated wind speeds. The last tornado that the National Weather Service gave an EF-5 rating to was the May 20, 2013, Moore, Oklahoma, tornado. That tornado had wind speeds of 200–210 miles per hour (320–340 kph). And it killed 24 people, injuring 212 others.

On October 6, 2025, after an extensive survey and analysis of wind damage, the National Weather Service ([NWS](https://www.weather.gov/media/fgf/Enderlin.pdf)) officially upgraded a tornado that hit Enderlin, North Dakota, to an EF-5 category. Thus ending the 12-year drought of EF-5 tornadoes. The NWS determined that the tornado had wind speeds greater than 210 miles per hour (340 kph). That estimate was based in part on a train derailment south of Enderlin. The survey also looked at tree damage that included debarking or _sandpapering_.

There were three deaths associated with the Enderlin tornado. The tornado largely struck a rural area, which helped keep the deaths and damages low. At one point, the tornado was more than a mile (1.6 km) wide. Plus it was on the ground for more than 12 miles (19 km). It scoured the ground between Enderlin and Sheldon, North Dakota, a little after 11 p.m. local time.

### Read the official NWS statement

The National Weather Service out of Grand Forks, North Dakota, [shared](https://www.weather.gov/media/fgf/Enderlin.pdf) the following public information statement on October 6:

> The National Weather Service in Grand Forks conducted additional surveys and worked extensively with wind damage experts to further investigate the 20 June 2025 Enderlin, ND tornado #1. The estimated maximum wind speed of the Enderlin, ND tornado #1 is greater than 210 mph (340 kph) and occurred during the time of the train derailment south of Enderlin, ND. The analysis involved forensic damage wind speed estimates for tipping several fully-loaded grain hopper cars and lofting of tanker cars, including one empty tanker car that was tossed about 475.7 ft (145 m). The maximum wind speed also correlates to the maximum strength on WSR-88D Storm-Relative Velocity data from KMVX.
> 
> Additional high-end damage indicators that have been reanalyzed and adjusted to include damage to the trees near the Maple River east of Enderlin and damage to the farmstead #2 on Hwy 46. Further analysis of the trees surrounding the Maple River show extensive tree damage throughout the entire river valley with only stubs of large branches or large trunks remaining and debarking with a ‘sandpapering’ effect prevalent. Trees with attached root ball displacements were noted, including one where the original location could not be determined. Wind damage expert analyses helped determine the damage at farmstead #2 to be complete destruction with the foundation considered to be swept clean, and debris swept downwind and scattered. However, issues surrounding the lack of proper anchoring will limit the overall rating in this area. Trees around the farmstead were also debarked, and saw root ball displacements.

### Video from the Enderlin tornado

Watch some videos from the night of the Enderlin tornado.

> [@foxweather](https://www.tiktok.com/@foxweather?refer=embed "@foxweather")TWISTER TERROR: Sirens blare as lightning illuminates nightmare-fuel tornado that left 3 dead in Enderlin, North Dakota over the weekend. Latest on the storm that lasted hundreds of miles. [#tornado](https://www.tiktok.com/tag/tornado?refer=embed "tornado") [#northdakota](https://www.tiktok.com/tag/northdakota?refer=embed "northdakota") [#enderlin](https://www.tiktok.com/tag/enderlin?refer=embed "enderlin") [#twister](https://www.tiktok.com/tag/twister?refer=embed "twister")
>

For a longer video of the Enderlin tornado, check out the 13-minute video below. Aaron Rigsby is a storm chaser who followed many of the storms that night. At the end of the video, Rigsby shares drone footage of the damage. The NWS viewed some of this footage to help make their decision to upgrade.

Bottom line: The 12-year-long drought of EF-5 tornadoes ended in 2025 after the NWS upgraded the Enderlin, North Dakota, tornado from June 2025 to an EF-5 tornado.

Mile-wide tornado that hit North Dakota in June was a monster EF5, the first in 12 years
========================================================================================

An EF5 tornado is one that reaches maximum wind speeds of over 200 mph. The tornado in June killed three people and derailed a number of train cars.

![Image 11](https://media.tegna-media.com/assets/CCT/images/ed81f8e7-327d-4c87-b421-1d07fa78f8a2/20251006T171207/ed81f8e7-327d-4c87-b421-1d07fa78f8a2_16x9.jpg) ![Image 12](https://media.tegna-media.com/assets/CCT/images/ed81f8e7-327d-4c87-b421-1d07fa78f8a2/20251006T171207/ed81f8e7-327d-4c87-b421-1d07fa78f8a2_750x422.jpg)

Credit: AP

The destruction caused by a tornado is visible in Moore, Oklahoma, on Wednesday, May 22, 2013. (AP Photo/Ted Shaffrey)

Author: Chris McCrory

Published: 1:49 PM EDT October 6, 2025

Updated: 1:49 PM EDT October 6, 2025

[![Image 13: Facebook](https://www.wnep.com/assets/shared-images/icons/facebook.svg)](https://www.facebook.com/dialog/share?app_id=201763624201505&display=popup&href=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.wnep.com%2Farticle%2Fnews%2Fnation-world%2Fnorth-dakota-tornado-june-upgraded-first-ef5-since-2013-national-weather-service%2F507-e1e671a6-cbaa-40e0-ac5c-188a333ae705&redirect_uri=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.wnep.com%2Farticle%2Fnews%2Fnation-world%2Fnorth-dakota-tornado-june-upgraded-first-ef5-since-2013-national-weather-service%2F507-e1e671a6-cbaa-40e0-ac5c-188a333ae705)

WASHINGTON — An EF5 tornado struck North Dakota this year, the National Weather Service confirmed Monday, marking the first tornado of that strength in more than a decade on American soil.

The incredibly strong twister touched down in Enderlin, North Dakota on June 20, the NWS [wrote in an advisory released on Oct. 6](https://www.weather.gov/media/fgf/Enderlin.pdf), using data gathered from the tornado's path in the nearly four months since it passed.

Meteorologists from the Grand Forks office headed into the field the morning following the tornado to examine the damage it had wreaked. It usually takes from days to weeks to determine the strength of a tornado by its wind speed, which meteorologists do by examining the damage to buildings and trees. This tornado took much longer to analyze because the damage it inflicted on the rail cars was unusual.

“In the last kind of 12 years, there’s been several strong tornadoes that have come close, but there haven’t been known damage indicators at that time to support the EF5 rating,” said Melinda Beerends, meteorologist in charge at the National Weather Service in Grand Forks. “It’s hard sometimes to get tornadoes to hit something.”

The Enderlin tornado carved a path over 12 miles long through a mostly rural part of the state. Enderlin, the city closest to its path, had a population of just under 900 people as of the 2020 census.

The tornado reached an estimated maximum wind speed over 210 mph, [killing three people and derailing several trains.](https://www.trains.com/pro/freight/north-dakota-storms-blamed-for-two-derailments/) Based on the path left behind, weather experts estimate the tornado just over a mile across.

The NWS report highlighted one empty tank car that was picked up by the winds and tossed nearly 500 feet away. [An empty tank car can weigh between around 50,000 and 90,000 lbs.](https://www.vtg.com/products-and-services/fleet/fleet-overview/tank-wagons)

Meteorologists use a tool known as the Enhanced Fujita Scale to determine how strong a tornado is after the fact. By looking at damage caused by the winds and other measurements taken during the storm, weather experts are able to classify a tornado based on wind speed.

The scale goes from EF0 tornadoes, which have wind speeds below 85 mph, to EF5 twisters, which have maximum wind speeds above 200 mph.

When was the last EF5 tornado?
------------------------------

The last EF5 tornado in the U.S. touched down in 2013, ravaging the area of Moore, Oklahoma. That tornado killed 25 people.

The tornado in June was strong enough to literally strip the bark from trees in its path, when it didn't rip the trees from the ground outright. The NWS noted in its advisory that damage was found throughout the valley where the tornado ripped through.

"Further analysis of the trees surrounding the Maple River show extensive tree damage throughout the entire river valley with only stubs of large branches or large trunks remaining and debarking with a “sandpapering” effect prevalent," the report reads. "Trees with attached root ball displacements were noted, including one where the original location could not be determined."

_The Associated Press contributed to this story._

Tornado outbreak and derecho of June 19–22, 2025

Radar loop of the derecho as it passed over North Dakota, Minnesota and other states and Ontario, Canada on June 20 through the night of June 21.

Meteorological history
DurationJune 19–22, 2025
Tornado outbreak
Tornadoes40
Maximum ratingEF5 tornado
Highest windsTornadic – >210 mph (340 km/h) (Enderlin, North Dakota EF5 on June 20)
Largest hail4 in (10 cm) near the Jamestown Dam on June 20th[1]
Derecho
Highest gusts120 mph (190 km/h) (Beltrami County, Minnesota)[2]
Maximum rainfall6.5 in (170 mm) (Chenango County, New York)[3]
Overall effects
Fatalities7 (6 tornadic, 1 from downburst)
Injuries>4
Damage$875 million (2025 USD)
Areas affectedNorthern United States (Great Plains), Southern Canada, Northeastern United States
Part of the tornado outbreaks of 2025
A significant [tornado outbreak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak "Tornado outbreak") and associated powerful [derecho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derecho "Derecho") caused major damage across the northern [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") and parts of southern [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada "Canada") on June 19–22, 2025. At least one other tornado was confirmed in [North Dakota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Dakota "North Dakota") the same day.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-DAT-4) The following day, the National Weather Service in Grand Forks confirmed that [a powerful tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Enderlin_tornado "2025 Enderlin tornado"), later rated EF5 a few months after, killed three people east of [Enderlin, North Dakota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enderlin,_North_Dakota "Enderlin, North Dakota").[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-5) The derecho also produced hurricane-force winds across Montana, North Dakota, Minnesota, and South Dakota, with the highest confirmed wind gust reaching 120 mph (190 km/h). Many tornadoes touched down in the Canadian province of [Saskatchewan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saskatchewan "Saskatchewan") as well. The same system produced another squall line that produced damaging wind, several downburst, and flash flooding in southern [Ontario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ontario "Ontario") on June 21 with one person being killed by a downburst.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-NTP-6)[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-CPnug-7) This line of storms would push into northern [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_/(state/) "New York (state)") early on June 22 and spawn a deadly EF1 tornado that killed three people in [Clark Mills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clark_Mills,_New_York "Clark Mills, New York").[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-DAT-4)[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-CMsurvey-8) It also caused widespread wind damage and flash flooding.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-CMcleanup-9)[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-cmnyt-10) In all, the storm system caused seven fatalities and produced 40 tornadoes, causing $875 million in damages.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-11) The outbreak saw the first EF5-rated tornado in over 12 years. Meteorological synopsis ----------------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Meteorological synopsis")\] The [Storm Prediction Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Storm_Prediction_Center "Storm Prediction Center") (SPC) had been monitoring favorable conditions for storm development in the Northern Plains/Upper Midwest region since June 18, noting limited low-level moisture and instability with modest wind shear yet steep [lapse rates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lapse_rate "Lapse rate") allowing for the development of weak thunderstorms in the area, which could in turn create a threat for isolated wind gusts and large hail.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-12) Although an upper-level [ridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ridge_/(meteorology/) "Ridge (meteorology)") was present throughout this region on June 19, a weak mid-level [shortwave trough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shortwave_/(meteorology/) "Shortwave (meteorology)") moved over the [Canadian Prairies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Prairies "Canadian Prairies") which, in combination with a strengthening low-level jet and the advection of warm, moist air, allowed for robust thunderstorm development with the primary threat being large hail and isolated strong wind gusts.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-13) [![Image 3: The National Weather Service Storm Prediction Center outlined a moderate SPC outlooks issued at 01Z, about three hours before the tornado touched down. A [wind-driven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derecho "Derecho") moderate risk was issued for the area, although the possibility of a strong tornado was mentioned.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-14) On June 15, the [Storm Prediction Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Storm_Prediction_Center "Storm Prediction Center") (SPC) noted on its Day 6 outlook that a shortwave, mid-level ridge was forecasted to traverse into the upper [Mississippi River valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_River "Mississippi River") and remain over the region as mid-level heights increase. Beneath the ridge, a moist and unstable airmass was expected to be in place from the lower to mid-Missouri Valley, northeastward into the western [Great Lakes region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Lakes_region "Great Lakes region"). Instability and deep-layer shear were sufficient for a localized severe threat, though uncertainties remained on where the greatest potential for convection would be.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-:5-15) A seasonally strong mid-level trough was forecast to eject over the Northern Plains on June 20, which featured moderate upper-level divergence to promote lift and shear support.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-:5-15) The [Storm Prediction Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Storm_Prediction_Center "Storm Prediction Center") (SPC) Day 2 outlook mentioned that "a small area of uncapped and very unstable air mass, perhaps over northeast SD and southeast ND. Although they were initially elevated, the strengthening low-level jet and isentropic/geostrophic ascent contributed to eroding the convective inhibition that was in place, allowing them to become more surface-based.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-:3-17) Additionally, a nearby frontal boundary provided extreme [storm-relative helicity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Storm-relative_helicity "Storm-relative helicity") which further supported surface-based shear and streamwise vorticity as well as development of rotation or mesocyclogenesis within the supercells.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-:3-17) Confirmed tornadoes ------------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025&action=edit§ion=4 "Edit section: Confirmed tornadoes")\]

### Enderlin, North Dakota \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025&action=edit§ion=9 "Edit section: Enderlin, North Dakota")\]

This large, violent, and deadly tornado touched down at 11:02 p.m. CDT south of Enderlin, initially snapping tree branches at EF0 intensity. The tornado intensified and widened as it moved northeastward across County Road 55 through open fields. The tornado then impacted the ADM Edible Bean Specialties facility at the corner of 136th Avenue SE and County Road 136 at EF2 strength, snapping large trees and destroying an outbuilding.[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-DAT2-49) The tornado then rapidly intensified as it continued northeastward, reaching EF5 intensity as it crossed [CPKC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Pacific_Kansas_City "Canadian Pacific Kansas City")'s [Elbow Lake Subdivision](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elbow_Lake_Subdivision "Elbow Lake Subdivision") southeast of Enderlin, derailing several train cars on a stopped freight train, including one empty tanker car that was thrown 475.5 feet (144.9 m) south of [ND 46](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Dakota_Highway_46 "North Dakota Highway 46").[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-:22-50) Initially, this damage was left unrated, but further analysis determined that there was forensic damage of the lofting of empty tanker cars weighing up to 72,000 pounds (33,000 kg) and tipping over fully loaded grain hopper cars weighing up to 286,000 pounds (130,000 kg) each. Based on this, the rating for this location was upgraded to EF5 with wind speeds greater than 210 mph (340 km/h) on October 6, 2025, the first F5/EF5 tornado to occur in North Dakota since the [Fargo tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fargo_tornado "Fargo tornado") exactly 68 years prior.[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-:22-50) Continuing north, the tornado blew over a cell tower, damaged crop fields, and snapped large trees, debarking some of them. A farmhouse was also swept away, and nearby outbuildings were destroyed. Crossing the highway, two houses were particularly devastated, with two fatalities occurring in the area. The first was swept away while the other was leveled.[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-:1-51) The tornado then began to turn northwest, leveling another home, which caused another fatality, and bending over tall steel electrical transmission towers before weakening and dissipating at 11:21 p.m. CDT.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-DAT-4) Overall, the tornado was on the ground for 19 minutes, had a path length of 12.10 miles (19.47 km), and reached a peak width of 1.05 miles (1.69 km). The tornado was the first to be rated EF5 on the [Enhanced Fujita scale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enhanced_Fujita_scale "Enhanced Fujita scale") since the [Moore, Oklahoma, tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_Moore_tornado "2013 Moore tornado") on May 20, 2013,[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-52) and was the first F5/EF5 tornado to occur in North Dakota since the [Fargo tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fargo_tornado "Fargo tornado") exactly 68 years prior.[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-53) ### Clark Mills–Clinton, New York \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025&action=edit§ion=10 "Edit section: Clark Mills–Clinton, New York")\]

The same line of thunderstorms associated with the earlier derecho continued to move across the [Northern United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_United_States "Northern United States") and Southern [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada "Canada"), reaching [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_/(state/) "New York (state)") by the early morning of June 22.[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-cmfox-54) This deadly QLCS tornado formed along a kink in this line, affecting the hamlet of [Clark Mills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clark_Mills,_New_York "Clark Mills, New York"), where three people were killed. The tornado first touched down within Clark Mills and moved southwestward through the hamlet, where it snapped or uprooted many trees.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-DAT-4)[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-CMsurvey-8) In this area, three people were killed when downed trees cut through and crushed their houses. In one house, six-year-old twin girls were killed by a tree that sliced through it, and a 50-year-old woman was killed in another location when a tree fell through the roof and crushed one end of her home; all victims were pronounced dead on the scene.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-cmnyt-10)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-CMcleanup-9) Overall, this made the tornado the second-deadliest in New York state history.[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-55) The tornado then turned sharply to the south, destroying a historic [grist mill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grist_mill "Grist mill") near [Oriskany Creek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oriskany_Creek "Oriskany Creek") with nearby heavy machinery being tossed into the creek. Continuing south, it began to move through more rural areas, causing more tree damage before turning southeast and dissipating.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-DAT-4)[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-CMsurvey-8) While a [tornado warning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_warning "Tornado warning") was issued for south-central [Oneida County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oneida_County,_New_York "Oneida County, New York") due to radar-indicated rotation,[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-56) the tornado initially formed outside of the polygon in an area that was just under a severe thunderstorm warning, although it did have a tornado possible tag. This was due to the warning being for another EF1 tornado that formed around the same time to the west of this one. Additionally, the rotation was assessed as being much farther south than it actually was.[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-57) This meant that not all of Clark Mills’ residents, including the three victims and their families, received the warning; many residents confirmed that they did not receive any warning. The early-morning time of this tornado also meant that most people were asleep as it touched down, so the warning may not have been able to reach them. It was further clarified that the [recent staffing cuts to NOAA and the NWS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NOAA_in_the_second_Trump_administration "NOAA in the second Trump administration") did not affect the [Binghamton office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Weather_Service_Binghamton,_New_York "National Weather Service Binghamton, New Severe thunderstorms moved into southern [Ontario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ontario "Ontario") on the evening of June 21 and the early morning of June 22, causing widespread wind damage and several [downbursts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Downburst "Downburst"). The [Samuel de Champlain Provincial Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_de_Champlain_Provincial_Park "Samuel de Champlain Provincial Park"), a popular summer camping spot, was particularly affected by an EF2-rated downburst; hundreds were left stranded due to flash flooding and a particularly strong downburst which downed trees and power lines, blocking off roads, and injured several people.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-NTP-6)[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-CPnug-7)[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-CPbay-62)[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-63) Similar severe weather effects were felt in other areas, such as [Algonquin Provincial Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algonquin_Provincial_Park "Algonquin Provincial Park"), where two separate downbursts occurred in the area. One of the two caused a tree to fall on a tent, injuring a boy camping with his mother.[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-64)[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-65)[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-66) Finally, in [Mallorytown, Ontario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Front_of_Yonge "Front of Yonge"), another downburst uprooted several trees, one of which fell on a tent occupied by a father with his young child; the father was killed while the child survived with serious but non-life-threatening injuries.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-NTP-6)[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-cbcMT-67) Several municipalities declared states of emergency due to the "devastation" brought by the severe storms.[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-68) Several downbursts were reported in [Quebec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quebec "Quebec") on the nighth of June 23.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-NTP-6) Overall, the downbursts in Canada caused one fatality and at least four injuries.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-NTP-6) This same line of storms also pushed into [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_/(state/) "New York (state)") on June 22, causing severe wind gusts, some up to 70 mph (110 km/h), which downed trees and power lines. This resulted in blocked roads and loss of power in the region.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-CMsurvey-8)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-CMcleanup-9) Additionally, rain brought by the storms caused localized flooding.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-cmnyt-10)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-CMcleanup-9) Extreme rainfall prompted a rare [flash flood emergency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flash_flood_emergency "Flash flood emergency") for six hours for [Chenango County, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chenango_County,_New_York "Chenango County, New York") as approximately 6.5 in (170 mm) of rain fell.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-cmnyt-10)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-bgmprecip-3) Many people were stranded by flood waters as they flooded creeks, roadways, and homes.[\[67\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-69)[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-cmfox-54) By[Reet Kaur](https://watchers.news/author/reet-kaur/) Saturday, June 21, 2025Saturday, June 21, 2025

[![Image 4: Google News Icon](https://www.google.com/s2/favicons?domain=news.google.com)Follow us on Google News](https://news.google.com/publications/CAAqBwgKMOKGjQswrNKeAw)

**A large tornado struck the town of Enderlin, North Dakota, at approximately 23:40 **local time (LT)** on June 20, 2025, killing three people and causing significant structural damage. The fatalities were confirmed by the Cass County Sheriff’s Office during a press conference held at 07:30 LT on June 21.**

![Image 5: YouTube video](https://i.ytimg.com/vi/vlfnTDd1WNA/hqdefault.jpg)

A deadly tornado impacted rural Cass County, North Dakota, at 23:40 LT on June 20. The Cass County Sheriff’s Office confirmed three fatalities in the area near Enderlin, two men and one woman, discovered at two separate locations following the storm.

Emergency services were dispatched after reports of damage, with storm chasers initially locating two deceased individuals. A third victim was later found by the Enderlin Fire Department at another site.

![Image 6: YouTube video](https://i.ytimg.com/vi/E1CzQuYRq10/hqdefault.jpg)

Search and welfare checks were conducted throughout the night by multiple agencies, including the Enderlin and Alice Fire Departments, Cass County deputies, Casselton and Lisbon ambulance services, the North Dakota Highway Patrol, and the Red River Valley UAS Unit.

No additional injuries have been reported. Extensive structural damage was confirmed, including destroyed homes and downed infrastructure, and a train that was overturned.

![Image 7: YouTube video](https://i.ytimg.com/vi/SzwEzQmGzNw/hqdefault.jpg)

This event marks the first tornado in North Dakota to cause at least two fatalities since the F4 tornado that struck Elgin on July 4, 1978, the first in a 47-year span. The tornado is being assessed by the NWS.

![Image 9: YouTube video](https://i.ytimg.com/vi/r7_w9Dht3d4/hqdefault.jpg)

The Enderlin tornado was part of a broader outbreak of severe weather affecting southeastern North Dakota and western Minnesota. The NWS received reports of tornadoes in Cass, Barnes, Ransom, and Stutsman counties.

Confirmed tornado sightings included locations near Eckelson, Urbana, Fort Ransom, and Davenport. Around 22:50 LT, a potentially destructive tornado was reported in Foster County, with another near Davenport at 23:50 LT, moving toward Oxbow.

![Image 11: YouTube video](https://i.ytimg.com/vi/h8-M4eU3oVU/hqdefault.jpg)

Wind gusts associated with the storm system reached up to 178 km/h (111 mph) near Luverne, North Dakota, and 170 km/h (106 mph) in Bemidji, Minnesota.

Additional weather hazards included hail up to 76 mm (3 inches) in diameter in Jamestown and portions of northwestern Minnesota. The NWS issued Tornado Watch 448, active until 03:00 LT on June 21, covering 14 counties in the region.

Power outages peaked at over 30 500 customers in southeastern North Dakota and 54 600 in Minnesota — approximately 200 000 people. As of 15:26 UTC on June 21, outages had been reduced to 22 876 customers in North Dakota and 27 040 in Minnesota.

NWS meteorologist Timothy Lynch described the outbreak as among the most widespread and impactful in his decade-long tenure with the service. A full damage survey and EF ratings for all tornadoes involved are pending.

https://twitter.com/narendra\_rawat1/status/1936326390715977983

The SPC reported 13 tornadoes in North Dakota on June 20, in Stutsman, Cass, Barnes, and Ransom counties.

![Image 1](https://media-cdn.socastsrm.com/wordpress/wp-content/blogs.dir/2431/files/2025/06/510886052-1294793252646627-534774141421899303-n.jpg)

Tornado near Sanborn, N.D. (Max Mueller/KVRR)

ENDERLIN, N.D. (KFGO) – Three people are dead after a tornado outbreak overnight.

Storm spotters located two people who were killed in a tornado near Enderlin, North Dakota around 11:40 p.m. Friday. While investigating the deaths, Enderlin Fire was dispatched to another address, and firefighters found another person who had been killed in the tornado.

Alice and Enderlin firefighters, Casselton and Lisbon Ambulance, Cass County Deputies, North Dakota Highway Patrol troopers, and the Red River UAS team searched the area and conducted welfare checks. No one else was injured.

National Weather Service Meteorologist Timothy Lynch says several tornadoes touched down in Stutsman, Barnes, Ransom, and Cass Counties.

“We can’t really rate it until we see what kind of damage it produced,” Lynch says. “However, from what I saw on radar and first hand accounts that were sent to us via video, they look like they could potentially be very strong tornadoes.”

Multiple structures were destroyed.

The National Weather Service is assessing damage to determine exactly how many tornadoes touched down and their severity.

High winds ripped roofs off homes, tipped semis, and uprooted trees.

“Radar-indicated winds upwards of 110 miles-per-hour and several reports from NDAWN, personal weather stations reported 80, 90, 100 miles-per-hour winds,” Lynch says. A 106 mph gust was recorded in Bemidji.

Strong storms were behind the supercells that produced tornadoes in west-central North Dakota. National Weather Service Meteorologist James Telken in Bismarck says the line produced straight-line winds over 100-miles-per-hour, as well as a few isolated tornadoes.

The winds knocked down powerlines across the region. As of Saturday morning, 30,510 customers were without power in the southeast part of North Dakota. Over 54,600 Minnesota customers were without power in the north-central part of the state, with over 22,500 of those in Beltrami county.

![Image 2](https://media-cdn.socastsrm.com/wordpress/wp-content/blogs.dir/2431/files/2025/06/image0-1-225x300.jpeg)

Downed power lines south of Alice, N.D. (photo courtesy Greg Kempel)

Hail up to 3in in diameter was reported in Jamestown and in northwest Minnesota. .

In Fargo, damage was limited to a few broken tree branches. Several underpasses flooded as a result of the heavy rainfall.

Lynch says last night’s outbreak is one of the most active storms he’s seen in his 10 years with the Weather Service.

“In my time here, this has probably been one of the more widespread severe events, and definitely one of the most profound.”

([North Dakota Monitor](https://northdakotamonitor.com/)) – The National Weather Service said that a tornado that touched down in Enderlin on June 20 had been upgraded to an EF5, the most severe category of tornado. EF5 tornadoes have top wind speeds exceeding 200 mph.

The Enderlin tornado is believed to be the first EF5 in the United States since 2013, according to the [National Weather Service website.](https://www.spc.noaa.gov/faq/tornado/f5torns.html)

The Governor’s Office in September submitted a separate request for federal disaster relief for August storms, which is still under review. The storm caused an estimated $6 million in damage, especially to electrical infrastructure.

The state has requested assistance for Barnes, Grand Forks, Griggs, Kidder, Nelson, Steele and Stutsman counties.
